introduction_markdown: Multiple choice paper (0560 History 1, June 2020, Ordinary Level, Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board). One and a half hours. Answer ALL the 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D: mark only one answer for each question (more than one answer scores zero for that question). The paper has three parts, all compulsory: Section A, Cameroon since 1850 (questions 1-25); Section B, Africa since 1870 (excluding Cameroon) (questions 26-40); Section C, World Diplomacy since 1870 (questions 41-50).
enonce_intro_markdown: **Multiple choice questions** - choose the one correct answer, A, B, C or D. Section A: Cameroon since 1850 (questions 1-25). Section B: Africa since 1870 (excluding Cameroon) (questions 26-40). Section C: World Diplomacy since 1870 (questions 41-50).
incertitudes: Page de garde vérifiée : « 0560 HISTORY 1 », JUNE 2020, ORDINARY LEVEL, Multiple Choice Question Paper, One and a half hours, « Answer ALL the 50 questions » (50 questions imprimées, aucune section à choix, toutes obligatoires). Sections imprimées : A Cameroon since 1850 (Q1-25), B Africa since 1870 excluding Cameroon (Q26-40), C World Diplomacy since 1870 (Q41-50). Aucune règle de choix : regles_choix et groupes sont vides (identique dans le seul fichier du dossier).

PDF avec une couche texte très bruitée (OCR du scan) mais lu page par page en image. Les filigranes et publicités (gcerevision.com, Kawlo, « for more free gce questions... ») n'ont pas été recopiés ; aucune figure dans ce sujet : figures vide.

Fautes d'impression corrigées à la transcription sans changer le sens : « Aymerick » (Aymerich) laissé tel quel dans l'énoncé de la Q7 et corrigé dans le corrigé ; « Lyttleton » (Lyttelton) laissé dans l'énoncé de la Q15 ; « Tripple » (Triple) à la Q41, « Hammariskjold » à la Q49, « diarrhear » (diarrhoea) à la Q50, « implimented » (implemented) à la Q30, « dimilitarised » (demilitarised) à la Q44, « Misc cn Valeur » (Mise en Valeur) à la Q18, « Peninsular » laissé tel quel (Q25, Q49), noms propres mal séparés ou en minuscule (Kuva Likenye, Tambe, Sembum II, Soppo Priso, Captain Moore, Perez de Cuellar). L'énoncé de la Q18 imprime « was:.. » (recopié « was ... »).

Q8 : deux explications (guerre sur plusieurs fronts, absence de renforts depuis l'Allemagne, liée au blocus) sont données par les manuels ; question passée en OUVERTE (aucune lettre désignée), options recopiées dans l'énoncé, réponse visée B (guerre sur plusieurs fronts).

Q9 : le motif de l'échec de la vente aux enchères de Londres (1922) n'est pas donné de façon univoque par les sources scolaires (prix élevés, faible intérêt des investisseurs britanniques, protestations locales) ; question passée en OUVERTE, réponse visée B (prix élevés). Détail du corrigé à vérifier par un historien : vente de 1924 avec retour de la plupart des plantations à leurs anciens propriétaires allemands.

Faits à faible marge d'incertitude (QCM conservés, clé déduite du programme et par élimination) : Q6 (première plantation allemande à Victoria : les manuels placent les premières plantations au pied du mont Cameroun, autour de Victoria, Bota et Bimbia ; formulation prudente dans le corrigé) ; Q11 (révolte gbaya de la fin des années 1920 : le corrigé ne donne ni date précise ni nom de chef) ; Q19 (Mayi Matip, qui s'est rallié au régime Ahidjo : date de ralliement non précisée) ; Q23 (« Green Revolution » : datée seulement des années 1970 dans le corrigé) ; Q24 (le sujet dit « early 2000s » mais l'opération Épervier date de 2006) ; Q15 (l'option B, création de la Southern Cameroons House of Assembly, est aussi un effet de la constitution de 1954 : l'option A, statut quasi régional, est la réponse classique) ; Q22 (l'option D, POWERCAM, a aussi disparu après l'unification, mais plus tard : la House of Chiefs reste la réponse attendue) ; Q30 (« assimilado » est une politique portugaise : seul l'Angola convient, mais « successfully » est une exagération : l'assimilation n'a touché qu'une petite minorité) ; Q36 (la Guinée de 1958 : rupture brutale avec la France, sans guerre) ; Q41 (l'alliance franco-russe de 1894 avait déjà brisé l'isolement de la France, mais la date de 1904 désigne l'Entente cordiale) ; Q48 (la Health Organisation de la SDN a aussi eu un successeur, l'OMS : l'OIT est la seule institution directement reprise) ; Q17 (de Gaulle est donne comme l'auteur de la visite de remerciement a Douala en octobre 1940 ; Leclerc, qui a conduit le ralliement d'aout 1940, pourrait aussi etre evoque par un manuel : cle conservee) ; Q28 (Stanley est qualifié de « trader » dans le sujet alors que c'est un explorateur au service de Léopold II). À relire par un historien avant mise en avant.
Aucun calcul numérique dans ce sujet (histoire) : rien à recalculer avec Python.
Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 8, 9. Réponses visées : Q8 B (guerre sur plusieurs fronts), Q9 B (prix élevés), toutes deux à relire par un historien.

Seconde passe faite : les 5 pages du PDF ont été relues en image et les 50 questions résolues une deuxième fois indépendamment ; énoncés et options conformes au sujet (hors fautes d'impression corrigées), aucune clé modifiée.

questions.enonce_markdown: The European missionary often associated with the founding of Victoria in 1858 was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Victoria (today Limbe) was founded in 1858 by the English Baptist missionary Alfred Saker of the Baptist Missionary Society. Saker had been working on the island of Fernando Po, but the Spanish authorities, who took control there, would not allow Protestant missions, so he led a group of Christian converts and freed slaves to the Cameroon coast and settled them at the foot of Mount Cameroon. The town was named after Queen Victoria. John Clarke is remembered for his early exploration of the coast with the Baptist Missionary Society, and Joseph Merrick (a Jamaican Baptist missionary) for his work at Bimbia and Douala, but neither is credited with founding Victoria. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which European power established trading companies along the Cameroon coast in the period 1840s to 1850s?
questions.corrige_markdown: After the abolition of the slave trade, British merchants and trading houses (palm oil traders from ports such as Liverpool and Bristol, working through Fernando Po and the Bight of Biafra) set up trading posts and ships along the Cameroon coast, dealing with the Duala middlemen. German firms came later (for example Woermann in 1868 and Jantzen and Thormaehlen in 1875), the Portuguese had left the coast long before as slave traders, and France had no comparable commercial presence there at that time. The power asked for is therefore Britain. **Answer: A.**
themes: european trade on the cameroon coast

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the British Imperial Officer who was sent out in the 1880s to annex Cameroon but failed to do so.
questions.corrige_markdown: Edward Hewett was the British consul for the Bights of Benin and Biafra. He was sent to the Cameroon coast in 1884 to make treaties with the Duala chiefs and place the area under British protection, as the chiefs had asked in the Kings' Memorandum of 1879. He arrived in July 1884, a few days after the Germano-Duala Treaty of 12 July 1884 had been signed, so Britain lost the race and Cameroon became a German protectorate. Gustav Nachtigal was a German official: he was the one who succeeded in annexing the territory for Germany. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following events made Cameroon a German colony?
questions.corrige_markdown: Cameroon became a German protectorate (colony) through the Germano-Duala Treaty of 12 July 1884, signed by the Duala kings (King Bell and King Akwa) and the representatives of the German trading firms, and followed by Gustav Nachtigal's proclamation of the German protectorate. The other options do not have this effect: Julius von Soden arrived in 1885 as the first German governor, after the colony already existed; the Court of Equity was a British-inspired body that settled trade disputes between European traders and Duala chiefs; and the Kings' Memorandum (1879) was a petition by the Duala chiefs asking Britain for protection. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: The arrival of Julius Von Soden as German Governor
The establishment of the Court of Equity.
The signing of the Kings' Memorandum.
The signing of the Germano - Duala Treaty.

questions.enonce_markdown: The prominent Cameroonian traditional ruler who led an anti - German resistance that resulted in the killing of Gravenreuth in 1891 was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Chief Kuva Likenye of Buea, the Bakweri leader, resisted the German push inland from the coast. In November 1891 the Bakweri fighters ambushed and defeated a German expedition near Buea and killed its commander, Baron von Gravenreuth. The Germans later returned in force and the Bakweri were subdued. The other names in the list are not associated with the killing of Gravenreuth. **Answer: B.**
themes: indigenous resistance to german rule in cameroon

questions.enonce_markdown: In which of the following coastal towns did the Germans establish the first plantation?
questions.corrige_markdown: German plantation agriculture began in the mid-1880s on the fertile volcanic soils at the foot of Mount Cameroon, around Victoria (for example the plantations opened near Victoria, Bota and Bimbia by German companies). Among the towns listed, Victoria is the one that is usually named in textbooks as the site of the first German plantation. Tiko grew later as a plantation and port centre, and Douala was mainly the trading and administrative centre of the colony. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Below is a list of Allied Military Commanders who participated in the Cameroon campaign, 1914 - 1916. Select the name of the commander of the French Allied Forces.
questions.corrige_markdown: In the Cameroon campaign of 1914-1916 the Allied forces were British (under General Charles Dobell), French (under General Joseph Aymerich, printed "Aymerick"), and Belgian. Colonel Zimmermann was the German commander, and Von Raben was also a German officer, so these two cannot be "Allied" commanders. The commander of the French forces is therefore General Joseph Aymerich. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The most important reason for the German defeat in Cameroon during the First World War was ...

*Options as printed:* A) the Germans lacked foreign military support   B) the Germans faced a war on many fronts   C) the Germans wanted to avoid another bloody battle like Nsanakang   D) top German military officers resigned and changed sides
questions.corrige_markdown:
The small German force (the Schutztruppe under Colonel Zimmermann) was attacked from several directions at once: the British from Nigeria and from the sea, the French from Chad, the Congo and Gabon, and the Belgians from the south. It was outnumbered, cut off from Germany by the Allied naval blockade and finally retreated: the main body crossed into Spanish Guinea (Rio Muni) in early 1916, and the last German garrison, at Mora in the north, held out until February 1916. Options C and D are not accepted explanations (the Germans had in fact won the battle of Nsanakang in September 1914, and there was no mass change of sides by German officers). Options A and B are both given in textbooks: the many-front war is the answer most often intended, but the lack of reinforcements from Germany is closely linked to it, so the question is not clear-cut.

**Intended answer: B (the Germans faced a war on many fronts).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The main reason why the auction sale of German estates in Cameroon that was organised in London in 1922 failed was ...

*Options as printed:* A) inadequate business security   B) the high prices of the estates   C) the absence of the German investors   D) the creation of Custodian of Enemy Property
questions.corrige_markdown:
After the First World War the British administration of the former German plantations in Southern Cameroons was run through the Custodian of Enemy Property, and the estates were put up for sale at an auction in London in 1922. The sale did not succeed as expected. The reasons usually given are that the estates had run down since the war and were offered at high prices, so that few British investors were willing to buy, and that there was local opposition to the return of the land to foreign owners. The plantations were offered again later (a sale in 1924 is reported to have returned most of them to their former German owners). Textbooks do not all give the same single reason for the 1922 failure, so this question cannot be marked reliably with one letter.

**Intended answer: B (the high prices of the estates).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: An important provision of the Clifford Constitution of 1922 that provoked the creation of pressure groups in Southern Cameroons in the 1930s and the early 1940s was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Clifford Constitution of 1922 set up a Legislative Council in Lagos for Nigeria, with a few elected seats for Lagos and Calabar. Southern Cameroons, administered as part of Nigeria under the British Mandate, had no representative in that Council, so its people had no voice in the making of laws and in the use of revenue. This feeling of neglect led educated Southern Cameroonians to form pressure groups, such as the Cameroons Youth League (1940), to defend the interests of the territory. The quasi-regional status (B) only came with the Lyttelton Constitution of 1954. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: it encouraged the creation of political parties in Nigeria
it granted Southern Cameroons a quasi regional status
it divided Southern Cameroons into the Bamenda Province and the Cameroons Province
the non representation of Southern Cameroons in the Legislative Council in Lagos

questions.enonce_markdown:
Question 11 is based on this historical opinion: "The revolt did not only result in the killing of its leaders, most importantly, it led to the end of Fulbe abuses and the creation of French administrative units in the area", during the Mandate period.

The above statement best describes ...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Gbaya of eastern Cameroon had suffered from the domination and exactions of the Fulbe rulers, and from French demands for forced labour and taxes. Their revolt against French rule in the late 1920s was crushed and its leader was killed, but the French then reorganised the area into administrative units directly under French officers, which reduced the power of the Fulbe chiefs over the Gbaya. The mention of the "end of Fulbe abuses" points to the Gbaya, not to the Douala (coastal), the Nso (in British Cameroons) or the Bane (in the south). **Answer: A.**
themes: revolts in french cameroon under the mandate

questions.enonce_markdown: A prominent Cameroonian traditional ruler who resisted the French, following reorganisation of chieftaincy institutions, was exiled and later died in Yaounde in 1933 was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Sultan Ibrahim Njoya of the Bamum kingdom (famous for creating the Bamum script) clashed with the French authorities, who reduced his powers, reorganised the chieftaincy and undermined his authority. He was exiled to Yaounde in 1931 and died there in 1933. Charles Atangana, by contrast, cooperated with the Germans and then the French, and Sembum II ruled Nso in British Cameroons. **Answer: B.**
themes: french rule in cameroon under the mandate

questions.enonce_markdown: An internal reason for the growth of nationalism in British Southern Cameroons after the Second World War was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Internal reasons are causes that arise inside the territory, while external reasons come from outside. The role of the super powers (the USA and the USSR), the decolonisation campaign of the United Nations Organisation and the Atlantic Charter of 1941 are all external influences. The formation of trade unions, such as workers' unions among plantation workers in Southern Cameroons, was a local development that gave Southern Cameroonians a way to organise and express their grievances, and so helped nationalism to grow. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the decolonisation campaign of the UNO
the impact of the Atlantic Charter

questions.enonce_markdown: In which year did British Southern Cameroons become a UN Trust Territory?
questions.corrige_markdown: The League of Nations Mandate over British Cameroons was replaced by a United Nations Trusteeship in 1946, when the Trusteeship Agreement was approved by the UN General Assembly (December 1946). British Southern Cameroons, administered as part of Nigeria, then became a UN Trust Territory under British administration. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Lyttleton Constitution of 1954 was so important to British Southern Cameroons because ...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954 (printed Lyttleton) turned Nigeria into a federation and gave Southern Cameroons a quasi-regional status, so that it was no longer a simple province of Eastern Nigeria: it had its own Executive Council and its own legislature, with its capital at Buea. This is what makes it important. It did not grant independence (the territory became independent by joining Cameroon in 1961), and political parties already existed before 1954. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: it granted the territory a quasi regional status
it created the Southern Cameroons House of Assembly
it authorized the formation of political parties in Southern Cameroons

questions.enonce_markdown: In which Southern Cameroons town was a meeting held in 1959 to deliberate on the plebiscite questions?
questions.corrige_markdown: The Mamfe Conference of 1959 brought together the main Southern Cameroons leaders and parties to discuss the questions to be put to the voters in the United Nations plebiscite (in which the voters were to choose between joining Nigeria and joining the Republic of Cameroon). The town was Mamfe. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The French military official who visited Cameroon in 1940 to thank Cameroonians for their support of the Free French Movement was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: In August 1940 Cameroon rallied to the Free French led by General Charles de Gaulle, thanks to the action of Philippe Leclerc and other Gaullist officers. De Gaulle himself visited Douala in October 1940 to thank the people of Cameroon for their support. Leclerc was one of the officers who carried out the rallying, so he is not the one who came to thank Cameroonians. Richard Brunot was a colonial administrator and Pierre Boisson was a governor who stayed loyal to the Vichy regime in French West Africa: neither was the leader of the Free French. **Answer: C.**
themes: impact of world war two on africa

questions.enonce_markdown: The harsh French colonial policy which as a result of the Brazzaville Conference of 1944 was abolished in Cameroon in 1946 was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Brazzaville Conference (1944) recommended reforms of French colonial rule. As a result the indigenat (a special legal code that allowed colonial administrators to punish Africans quickly, without trial, for minor offences) was abolished in 1946. Assimilation was the policy of turning Africans into Frenchmen, association was the policy of ruling with the help of local chiefs, and mise en valeur was the economic exploitation of the colonies: none of these was abolished in 1946. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The UPC leader who eventually joined the Ahidjo government in the 1960s was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Theodore Mayi Matip, a UPC leader who stayed in the country, eventually rallied to the Ahidjo regime. Abel Kingue and Felix Moumie were UPC leaders who died in exile and never joined the government, and Paul Soppo Priso was a nationalist politician who was not a UPC leader. **Answer: B.**
themes: upc and french repression in cameroon

questions.enonce_markdown: The political party and its leader that led French Cameroon to independence in January 1960 was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: French Cameroon became independent on 1 January 1960 under Ahmadou Ahidjo, the leader of the Union Camerounaise (UC), who became its first President. Andre Marie Mbida (Democrats of Cameroon) was Prime Minister in 1957-1958 but had been replaced by Ahidjo; the UPC was banned in 1955 and fought a rebellion; Paul Soppo Priso led another party but not the country to independence. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: "How nice it is to meet our brothers". During which important conference did President Ahidjo make the above declaration?
questions.corrige_markdown: The Foumban Constitutional Conference was held on 17-21 July 1961, after the plebiscite, to work out the constitution of the new federation between the Republic of Cameroon and Southern Cameroons. President Ahmadou Ahidjo opened it, and his greeting to the delegates from Southern Cameroons, who were welcomed as brothers, is associated with that conference. The Bamenda and Mamfe meetings were gatherings of Southern Cameroons leaders, and the Yaounde meeting of August 1961 came after the Foumban talks. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An important West Cameroon institution that ceased to exist after the introduction of the unitary system of government in 1972 was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: After the referendum of 20 May 1972 the Federal Republic became the United Republic of Cameroon, a unitary state, and the institutions of the federated states were abolished. The West Cameroon House of Chiefs, an institution which existed only in West Cameroon, disappeared with the West Cameroon government and House of Assembly. The Cameroon National Assembly was kept as the single national assembly of the unitary state. The Cameroon Bank and POWERCAM were not political or constitutional institutions tied to the federal system. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: The West Cameroon House of Chiefs

questions.enonce_markdown: The political slogan of President Ahidjo aimed at encouraging greater agricultural productivity in Cameroon was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: In the 1970s President Ahidjo's government promoted the "Green Revolution" to increase food and cash-crop production and make the country self-sufficient in food. "Operation Feed the Nation" was a Nigerian campaign of the 1970s, "Operation Green Sahel" is a tree-planting programme against desertification in the north of Cameroon, not a slogan about farm productivity, and the New Deal Programme was the American economic recovery programme of President Roosevelt in the 1930s. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An important measure taken by the Biya administration to fight against corruption in Cameroon in the early 2000s was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Under President Paul Biya the government launched an anti-corruption campaign, with the creation of the National Anti-Corruption Commission and Operation Sparrowhawk (Epervier), in which former ministers and managers of public enterprises accused of embezzling public funds were arrested and prosecuted (from 2006). The 1996 Constitution, the bi-cameral legislature (Senate and National Assembly) and the creation of state universities in 1993 are institutional or educational reforms that have nothing to do with fighting corruption. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Arrest of embezzlers of public funds
Creation of six State Universities in 1993

questions.enonce_markdown: Which international organisation provided a peaceful settlement to the dispute between Cameroon and Nigeria over the Bakassi Peninsular?
questions.corrige_markdown: Cameroon took its dispute with Nigeria over the Bakassi Peninsula to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) at The Hague in 1994. The Court gave its judgment on 10 October 2002 and awarded Bakassi to Cameroon, and the settlement was then carried out peacefully through the Greentree Agreement of 2006, with United Nations help. The Security Council and the Secretariat did not judge the case, and the Trusteeship Council had no role since Cameroon was no longer a trust territory. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following was a political reason for the European scramble for Africa in the 19th Century?
questions.corrige_markdown: The scramble for Africa had economic reasons (raw materials, markets and investment), social reasons (land for settlers and for surplus population), religious and cultural reasons (spreading Christianity and European civilisation) and political reasons. The quest for national prestige and power, with rival European states wanting more colonies than their neighbours, is the political reason. The others are economic (A), social (C) and cultural (D). **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: The desire to spread their culture

questions.enonce_markdown: The World power that attended the Berlin West Africa Conference of 1884 to 1885 but failed to participate in the scramble and colonisation of Africa was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Berlin West Africa Conference (1884-1885) was attended by fourteen states, including the United States of America. The USA did not take part in the partition: it had no colony in Africa at that time (it was mainly interested in Liberia and in trade). Portugal and Spain both took part in the scramble and held colonies in Africa, and Switzerland did not take part in the conference. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the trader, whose company's activities greatly influenced the annexation of the Congo Basin by the Belgians.
questions.corrige_markdown: Henry Morton Stanley explored the Congo and, working for King Leopold II of the Belgians, signed treaties with chiefs and set up stations on behalf of the association that Leopold had founded to open the Congo basin (the International African Association and later the Congo association). This led to the Berlin Conference recognising the Congo Free State, as the personal property of Leopold II, in 1885. It passed to Belgium in 1908. Cecil Rhodes worked in southern Africa (British South Africa Company), De Brazza acted for France north of the Congo, and Karl Peters acted for Germany in East Africa. The question calls Stanley a trader, but he was an explorer working for Leopold's company. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The French colonial policy that made use of traditional rulers in the colonial administration after 1905 was ....
questions.corrige_markdown: After the failure of assimilation (turning Africans into Frenchmen), France moved in the early 20th century to a policy of association, in which local institutions were respected and traditional rulers were used as intermediaries and auxiliaries in the administration, while remaining under French control. Assimilation (A) did not use chiefs, and paternalism and differentiation are not the names of the French policy of the period. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In which of the following European colonies was the policy of Assimilado successfully implemented?
questions.corrige_markdown: The assimilado system was a Portuguese policy: an African could be recognised as an "assimilado" (a civilised person with the rights of a Portuguese citizen) if he could read and write Portuguese, had a job, and lived like a European. Of the colonies listed, only Angola was a Portuguese colony (Kenya and the Gold Coast were British, Senegal was French). In Angola a small minority of Africans obtained this status, so the policy can only be said to have worked for a very small group. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The African revolt of the 1890s often linked to the defeat of an imperial European power was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Ethiopia (Abyssinia) under Emperor Menelik II defeated the Italian army at the Battle of Adwa on 1 March 1896 and kept its independence, one of the few cases of a European imperial power defeated by Africans in the 1890s. The Mau Mau revolt in Kenya belongs to the 1950s, the Maji Maji rising in German East Africa to 1905-1907, and the Mandinka resistance of Samori Toure was crushed by the French in 1898. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which one of the following was a major reason for African resistance to European colonial rule?
questions.corrige_markdown: Land was the basis of the life of African communities (farming, grazing, burial places and chieftaincy), so the seizure of African lands by the colonisers for settlement, plantations and mining was the most important and most widespread cause of resistance. Plantations, the use of porters and the loss of the middlemen's monopoly of trade were also grievances, but they were either consequences of the loss of land or concerned only some groups and areas. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: The use of Africans as porters
Abolition of middle man monopoly of trade

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify an African colony which as a result of German defeat in the First World War became a Mandated territory of the League of Nations.
questions.corrige_markdown: After Germany lost the First World War, the League of Nations put its colonies under the control of the victorious powers as Mandates. German East Africa became Tanganyika, a British Mandate (with Rwanda-Urundi going to Belgium). Southern Rhodesia and the Gold Coast were British colonies and Mozambique was a Portuguese colony, so none of them had been German. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An important political effect of the Second World War on Africans was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Loss of lives and property, displacement of populations and inflation were social and economic effects. The war's main political effect was the growth of nationalist feeling: African soldiers who had fought for the Allies returned with new ideas and experience, the colonial powers were weakened, and the Atlantic Charter and the United Nations encouraged claims for self-determination. **Answer: D.**
themes: impact of world war two on africa

questions.enonce_markdown: Which African city hosted an important wartime conference in 1943?
questions.corrige_markdown: The Casablanca Conference was held in January 1943 in Casablanca (Morocco), where the American President Franklin Roosevelt and the British Prime Minister Winston Churchill met to plan the Allied strategy after the North African landings, and announced the policy of "unconditional surrender" of the Axis powers. The other cities listed did not host an important wartime conference of the Allies in 1943. **Answer: C.**
themes: impact of world war two on africa

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify a French African colony which did not witness a peaceful decolonisation process.
questions.corrige_markdown: Ivory Coast, Niger and Senegal became independent in 1960 through negotiation and with continuing close ties with France. Guinea under Sekou Toure was the exception: in the referendum of September 1958 on de Gaulle's constitution it voted "No" and became independent in October 1958. France reacted angrily, withdrew its administrators and equipment suddenly and cut its aid, so the process was marked by a bitter break with France, although there was no war of independence. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Select the pair of African colonial territories in which nationalism became increasingly violent after 1945.
questions.corrige_markdown: In Kenya nationalism turned violent in the Mau Mau revolt (1952-1960) against British settler rule and land policy, and in Mozambique African nationalists of FRELIMO began an armed struggle against Portuguese rule in 1964. In the other pairs at least one territory moved to independence peacefully: the Gold Coast (Ghana, 1957), Sierra Leone, Guinea, Nigeria and Senegal. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Civil wars occurred in the following African countries after independence except ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Nigeria had the Biafran civil war (1967-1970), Congo had a civil war and secession crisis soon after independence in 1960, and Liberia suffered long civil wars in 1989-2003. Senegal has had a long, low-level separatist conflict in the Casamance region, but it did not experience a national civil war like the others, so it is the exception. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A Southern African country that practised the policy of racial discrimination and white minority rule right up to 1980 was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Southern Rhodesia was ruled by its white minority, which under Ian Smith made the Unilateral Declaration of Independence in 1965 to avoid black majority rule. After years of guerrilla war and the Lancaster House agreement, majority rule came and the country became independent as Zimbabwe in April 1980. Northern Rhodesia (Zambia) and Nyasaland (Malawi) became independent in 1964 and Mozambique, a Portuguese colony, in 1975. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the African country in which the first summit of the African Union (AU) took place in 2002.
questions.corrige_markdown: The African Union replaced the Organisation of African Unity and was launched at its first summit in Durban, South Africa, in July 2002, with the South African President Thabo Mbeki as its first chairperson. Its headquarters are in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, but the launching summit was in South Africa. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The European alliance system which ended the isolation of France in 1904 was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: France had been diplomatically isolated after its defeat of 1871. In 1904 France and Britain signed the Entente Cordiale, an agreement that settled their colonial disputes (notably over Egypt and Morocco) and brought the two countries together; this ended France's isolation. The Triple Alliance was the alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy, the Triple Entente was formed later (1907, when Russia joined), and the Dual Alliance was the earlier Franco-Russian alliance of the 1890s. The question asks for the system of 1904. (The printed word "Tripple" was corrected to "Triple".) **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The European power that declared war on Serbia on 28th July 1914 leading to the outbreak of the First World War was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: After the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, Austria-Hungary sent an ultimatum to Serbia and declared war on it on 28 July 1914. The alliance system then drew in Russia, Germany, France and Britain. Germany declared war on Russia and France only in August, and Turkey and Bulgaria entered the war later. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the Peace Treaties of 1919 was imposed on Austria?
questions.corrige_markdown: The Paris Peace Conference produced a treaty for each defeated power: Versailles for Germany, Saint-Germain (September 1919) for Austria, Neuilly for Bulgaria, Trianon for Hungary (1920) and Sevres for Turkey (later replaced by the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923). The Treaty of St Germain reduced Austria to a small state, limited its army and forbade union with Germany. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A territory of the former German Empire that as a result of the Treaty of Versailles (1919) was demilitarised was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Treaty of Versailles ordered the demilitarisation of the Rhineland, the German territory west of the Rhine and a zone east of it: Germany could not keep troops or fortifications there, and the Allies were to occupy it for fifteen years. Hitler sent troops back into it in 1936. The Sudetenland belonged to Czechoslovakia, the Polish Corridor was given to Poland and Danzig became a Free City under the League of Nations. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The policy of the 1930s that aimed at granting territorial concessions to Axis powers with the hope of preventing war in Europe was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Appeasement was the policy followed mainly by Britain and France in the 1930s, under leaders like Neville Chamberlain, of giving in to the demands of Hitler and Mussolini (for example by accepting the German takeover of the Sudetenland at Munich in 1938) in the hope of avoiding another war. Isolationism was the American policy of staying out of foreign quarrels, while fascism and Nazism were the ideologies of Italy and Germany. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A European city that as a result of the Second World War was partitioned into zones of military occupation was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: At the end of the Second World War Germany was divided into four zones of occupation (American, British, French and Soviet), and Berlin, although it lay inside the Soviet zone, was also divided into four sectors. Rome, Prague and Warsaw were not partitioned into occupation zones. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The two cities that were linked by the HOT telephone line after the Cuban Missile Crisis of the 1960s to minimize the possibility of a nuclear war were ...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 showed how slow communication between the two super powers was. In 1963 the United States and the Soviet Union agreed to set up a direct communication link (the "hot line") between the White House in Washington and the Kremlin in Moscow, so that leaders could talk quickly in a crisis and avoid a nuclear war by accident. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Select the main organ of the League of Nations that was incorporated into the United Nations System as a Specialised Agency.
questions.corrige_markdown: The International Labour Organisation (ILO), created in 1919 with the League of Nations, continued after the League was dissolved and in 1946 became the first specialised agency of the United Nations. The Mandate Commission was replaced by the UN Trusteeship Council, and the work of the League's Health Organisation was taken over by a new body, the World Health Organization (1948), so only the ILO was carried over directly. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the UN Secretary General who was very instrumental in the peaceful settlement of the dispute between Cameroon and Nigeria over the Bakassi Peninsular.
questions.corrige_markdown: Kofi Annan, UN Secretary General from 1997 to 2006, encouraged the two presidents to accept the ruling of the International Court of Justice (2002), and set up the Cameroon-Nigeria Mixed Commission and the Greentree Agreement (2006) for its peaceful implementation. Boutros Boutros-Ghali (1992-1996), Dag Hammarskjold (1953-1961) and Javier Perez de Cuellar (1982-1991) served in other periods. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The following are symptoms of HIV/AIDS except ....
questions.corrige_markdown: HIV weakens the immune system, and typical signs of the disease include persistent diarrhoea, rapid weight loss, long-lasting skin rashes, fever, night sweats and repeated infections. Diabetes is a metabolic disease linked to blood sugar and is not a symptom of HIV/AIDS. **Answer: B.**
